headline: Over 100 factories halt production across Bangladesh due to severe gas shortage
summary: The crisis has severely impacted industries producing daily necessities, pharmaceuticals, ceramics, and steel, leading to significant production cuts and temporary closures, especially in Narayanganj, Narsingdi, and Chattogram.
details: Over 100 factories across Bangladesh have halted production in the past week due to a severe gas shortage, with many more experiencing significant output reductions. This crisis is particularly acute in Narayanganj, Narsingdi, and Chattogram, affecting gas-dependent small and large industries.

The affected sectors include daily necessities, pharmaceuticals, ceramics, and steel. Some factories are using alternative fuels like diesel to maintain limited operations, but this has substantially increased their production costs.

The gas supply crisis has intensified over the last month, with the past week seeing the most severe disruptions. Low gas pressure often forces workers to remain idle, impacting productivity and overall output.
Major industrial groups are heavily impacted. Meghna Group of Industries (MGI) has completely shut down production in 40 out of its 57 factories, primarily those producing daily necessities.

TK Group also reports most of its 28 factories are closed, with only one operating at a limited capacity in the Dhaka vicinity. Their electricity-dependent factories in northern, Jashore, and Khulna regions are suffering from 8-10 daily load shedding incidents.
ACI Limited has seen overall production decline significantly across its various plants, with some experiencing cuts of 30% to over 50%. Salt production, in particular, has been severely hampered.

Executive Director of ACI Limited, Kamrul Hasan, stated that both electricity problems and the inability to run generators due to gas shortages are causing substantial financial losses. Boiler-dependent factories have seen production plummet.
The impact extends to wholesale markets, with Narayanganj's Nitai Ganj, a major trading hub, reporting no sugar truck arrivals for three days. This has led to a BDT 7 per kg increase in sugar prices.

Edible oil production is also down. Meghna Edible Oil Refinery, capable of producing 2,500 tons daily, has been shut for three days. City Group's City Edible Oil Limited has seen its 2,500-ton daily capacity reduced to approximately 1,000 tons due to low gas pressure.
caption:

headline: Over 3.4 lakh SSC students scored GPA 4 to below 5, highlighting a mid-tier performance trend
summary: While overall pass rates and GPA-5 numbers declined, a significant portion of successful candidates achieved results in the mid-range, indicating a broader distribution of academic achievement.
details: The recent SSC and equivalent examination results show a significant decline in both the average pass rate and the number of GPA-5 recipients. This has shifted focus from just failures to the distribution of results among those who passed. A notable trend reveals that a large segment of successful students achieved mid-tier scores.

Specifically, over 3.43 lakh students, approximately 19% of the total examinees, scored in the GPA 4 to below 5 range. This group generally achieved an average of 70-79% marks in each subject. This figure is higher than the number of students who secured the top GPA-5.

The overall pass rate across nine general education boards, madrasa, and technical education boards stood at 62.25%, meaning nearly 38% of examinees did not pass. While the lower pass rate is a major talking point, analyzing the GPA tiers of successful students presents a more nuanced picture.

Out of more than 18.29 lakh examinees, only 6.38% (over 1.16 lakh students) achieved GPA-5, scoring 80-100% in each subject. In contrast, 18.79% of students fell into the GPA 4 to below 5 category, indicating a larger group just below the highest achievement level.

Further analysis shows 12.16% secured GPA 3.5 to below 4, and 12.35% achieved GPA 3 to below 3.5. These two mid-level tiers together account for nearly a quarter of all examinees. Additionally, 12.07% scored GPA 2 to below 3, while a mere 0.52% were in the GPA 1 to below 2 range.

Experts emphasize that a complete understanding of student learning outcomes requires more than just pass rates or GPA-5 numbers. Analyzing the distribution across various GPA levels offers clearer insights into learning quality, preparation, and evaluation results. Some students passed with very low marks, which could impact their future studies.

Weaknesses in English and Mathematics were particularly evident in this year's results, with pass rates in English falling below 80% in most general education boards. Education board officials believe poor performance in these compulsory subjects contributed to the overall decline in the pass rate. Significant differences were also observed in group-wise results, with the humanities section recording the lowest pass rate.

According to Md Mostafizur Rahman, Deputy Director of the Campaign for Popular Education, exam results do not solely determine a student's capability or future. He urged the government to conduct a detailed post-result analysis to identify areas, regions, and institutions where students are lagging. He also recommended special support programs for weak subjects like English and Mathematics, and development plans for institutions with zero pass rates, alongside improved teacher training and academic support.
